pedagogy.summary: Children measure two or three objects in standard units and then compare and order the results, recording with >, <, and =. The measurement-specific demand on top of number comparison is that a measurement is a number WITH a unit: 1 m is longer than 50 cm even though 1 < 50, so the numbers can only be compared once they are in the same unit (or represented on a common scale).
bestPractices: Measure first, then compare — the comparison is of the measured amounts, not of how the objects look.
Insist the unit travels with the number; make same-unit comparisons before ever mixing units.
Confront the bare-number trap deliberately (1 m vs 50 cm; 300 g vs 1 kg) so children see the number alone can mislead.
Connect >, <, = to the number-comparison children already do, reading the statement aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Order three measures by repeatedly picking the largest (or smallest), and use = only when the measures are genuinely equal.
keyRepresentations: Two measured bars/ribbons side by side with the symbol between them (45 cm > 32 cm)
A common-scale bar chart that lets 1 m and 50 cm be compared visually
An ordering strip: three containers arranged by measured capacity
The >, <, = symbols read as 'greater than / less than / equal to'
commonMisconceptions: Compares the bare numbers and ignores the units — '50 cm > 1 m because 50 is bigger than 1', or '300 g > 1 kg'.
Reverses the symbol — writes 32 > 45, pointing the 'mouth' the wrong way.
Orders by appearance rather than by the measured amounts.
Uses = loosely for measures that are merely close, not equal.

learn.summary: Children measure two or three objects in standard units, then compare and order the measured amounts and record using >, <, and =. The key demand beyond plain number comparison is that a measurement is a number WITH a unit: 1 m is longer than 50 cm even though 1 < 50, so the numbers can only be compared once they share a unit (or are shown on a common scale). Measure first, keep the unit travelling with the number, confront the bare-number trap deliberately, and use = only for genuinely equal measures.

activities.title: Measure, then place the symbol
feedback: If a learner writes 50 cm > 1 m because '50 is bigger', have them line both up on one shared ruler or convert to the same unit (1 m = 100 cm) so the metre visibly towers over the 50 cm; then re-record the true statement 1 m > 50 cm.
If the symbol is reversed (e.g. 32 > 45), re-anchor 'the open side faces the bigger amount' and have them read the statement aloud to check it matches what they mean.
When correct, confirm by reading the full statement aloud with the unit included, e.g. '45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres'.
activities.rationale: Measuring before comparing ties the symbol to a measured amount rather than appearance, and a deliberate unit-mismatch pair surfaces the bare-number trap so the 'keep the unit' idea is experienced, not just stated. An optional interactive version may let a child drag the symbol between two readings for immediate feedback and slide a mismatched pair onto one common ruler so the true sizes show.
sourceClaims: In measurement the concept of unit is crucial and unit size is critical: counting discrete items often convinces students that the size of what is counted does not matter, but for measurement the unit must always be considered — a number is meaningful only with its unit ('what are you counting?' -> 'centimeters'). The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship).
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, <, and =; this parallels comparing and ordering two-digit numbers with the same symbols.
learnerActions: Measure two objects in the same unit and write each measurement with its unit (e.g. a pencil case at 32 cm and a book at 45 cm).
Place >, <, or = between the two readings so the statement is true, then read it aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Check the symbol points its open side toward the larger amount.

Repeat with a mixed-unit pair, such as a 1 m ribbon and a 50 cm ribbon: before deciding, bring both to the same unit or line them up on one common ruler/scale, then record the true comparison (1 m > 50 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number together with its unit; you must compare the actual amounts, not the bare digits. When units differ, convert to a shared unit first: 1 m equals 100 cm, which is more than 50 cm, so 1 m > 50 cm even though 1 is a smaller number than 50.

activities.title: Order three measured things
feedback: If a learner orders by how things look, require the measured value to be written beside each object first, then re-order using only those numbers; discuss the case where looks and measures disagree.
If = is used for measures that are only close, ask them to compare the exact readings and decide whether they are truly equal or whether > or < is correct.
When units differ across the three items, prompt converting to a shared unit or placing them on one common scale before ordering.
activities.rationale: Writing the measured value beside each object forces attention onto the numbers, and a looks-vs-measures conflict case makes the measure-not-appearance point concrete. Three-way ordering extends two-way comparison and gives a natural place to discuss when = truly applies.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, <, and =; this parallels comparing and ordering two-digit numbers with the same symbols.
learnerActions: Measure three objects (e.g. three containers for capacity) and write the measured value, with its unit, next to each.
Arrange them from least to most by repeatedly picking the smallest remaining measured amount (or from most to least by repeatedly picking the largest remaining measured amount).
Include a case where how big the objects look disagrees with what they measure, and order by the measurements anyway.
Use = only between two measures that are genuinely equal, not merely close.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering is done on the measured amounts, not on appearance, and = is reserved for truly equal measures.

activities.title: Reference card for the symbols
feedback: Prompt the learner to read each statement aloud with units, confirming the words match the symbol.
Follow a reference check with an actual measure-and-compare task, since reading a fixed example does not by itself show whether the learner can choose and place the symbol for a new pair.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled example clarifies what the notation means and how it is read; it is a scaffold for understanding and should be paired with tasks where the learner makes and tests their own comparisons, especially mixed-unit ones. Reviewing a fixed example checks recognition of the notation but does not itself elicit independent production of a comparison.
learnerActions: Study a labelled example such as '45 cm > 32 cm' and say what >, <, and = mean ('greater than', 'less than', 'equal to').
Describe why the open side of the symbol faces the larger amount.
Explain in words why a mixed-unit statement like '1 m > 50 cm' is true even though 1 is smaller than 50 (because 1 m is 100 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Secures the meaning and reading of the >, <, = notation as support for making one's own comparisons.

constraints: Learners must measure first; comparison is of the measured amounts, not of how objects look.
The unit must travel with the number; make same-unit comparisons secure before mixing units.

Include at least one deliberate mixed-unit pair (e.g. 1 m vs 50 cm, 300 g vs 1 kg) where the bare-number guess is wrong, so the misconception is confronted and resolved by converting to a shared unit or using a common scale.
Reserve = for genuinely equal measures, not measures that are merely close.
A fixed labelled reference example clarifies notation but does not let the learner make and test their own comparisons; follow it with construction tasks.
Recognition or reference-only activities do not by themselves show that a learner can independently choose, point, and place the symbol for a new pair, including mixed-unit cases.
Explain mixed-unit comparisons by converting to a shared unit, not by a 'bigger unit wins' shortcut, which does not hold in general (e.g. 500 cm > 1 m).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: the original error-pattern example 'writes 50 cm > 1 m' was converted into corrected learner actions/feedback (the true comparison is 1 m > 50 cm). The incorrect form appears only as a described mistake to fix, never as a valid answer. Likewise '300 g > 1 kg' appears only as a flagged misconception (1 kg > 300 g).

The original recommendation framed the insight as '1 beats 50 because the unit behind the number is bigger'; this heuristic is not generally valid (a larger unit does not always yield a larger measurement), so the insight was reworded to compare amounts via conversion to a shared unit.
One source (UK National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the row; treated as a curriculum reference for the >, <, = recording convention, not as efficacy evidence.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue cannot rehearse choosing and placing the symbol'; these universal comparative-necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been removed. The retained objective point is only that recognition/reference-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a comparison.

probeDeeper: This one says 1 m and that one says 50 cm — which is longer? How do you know, when 50 is a bigger number than 1?
Read your statement aloud — does 32 > 45 say what you mean?
You put these three in that order — did you measure them, or go by how they look? Would measuring change anything?
When would you use the = sign for two of these measurements?
assess.correctAnswer: The child records correct comparisons with the symbol pointing to the smaller amount (45 cm > 32 cm), compares the mixed-unit pair by the actual amounts (1 m > 50 cm, not < ), orders the three by their measured values, and uses = only for genuinely equal measures.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares bare numbers, ignoring units: judges by the digits alone, so '50 cm > 1 m because 50 is bigger', or '300 g > 1 kg'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both on a common scale/unit so the true sizes show; reinforce that the unit travels with the number and comparison needs a shared unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 50 cm > 1 m, or orders a 1 m item below a 50 cm item; untroubled that the units differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Symbol reversal: points the > / < the wrong way, writing 32 > 45 — the 'open mouth' convention not secured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'the open side faces the bigger amount'; read the statement aloud and check it matches; borrow from number-comparison practice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The symbol opens toward the smaller number; may read it correctly aloud yet write it backwards.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by appearance, not by measuring: arranges objects by how big they look rather than by the measured amounts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require the measured value to be written by each object before ordering; compare a case where looks and measures disagree.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Skips or ignores the measurements when ordering; ranking follows perceived size and can contradict the numbers.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the bare numbers (50 cm > 1 m), reverses the symbol, or orders by appearance without measuring.
responseLevels.full: Records correct comparisons with the symbol pointed the right way, compares and orders by the actual amounts even when units differ, and uses = only for genuinely equal measures — explaining that the unit must be considered, not just the number.
responseLevels.partial: Compares and records correctly when the units match (45 cm > 32 cm) but is caught by a mixed-unit pair, or orders same-unit measures yet not across units — can do the routine case but not attend to the unit when it matters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler and set out a few objects, then some already-labelled measurement cards including a mixed-unit pair (e.g. a 1 m ribbon and a 50 cm ribbon, and a 45 cm vs 32 cm pair). Say: 'Measure these, then write which is bigger using the >, <, or = sign, and put these three containers in order from least to most.' Watch whether they attend to the units, which way the symbol points, and whether they order by measuring or by looks.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands that a measure is a number-with-a-unit compares 1 m and 50 cm correctly and points the symbol the right way; a child who does not writes 50 cm > 1 m (bare numbers), reverses the symbol, or orders by appearance — each visible in what they write and do.

The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship).
